variants.title: Read the state
variants.context: Closed: calls reach the dependency while outcomes are recorded. Open: calls fail fast without reaching it. Half-open: a small number of probes pass and decide whether to close or reopen.
variants.prompt: Calls are reaching the dependency and the breaker is recording timeouts in a window. Which state?
options: Closed.
Open.
Half-open.
optionFeedback: Closed measures normal calls.
Open blocks calls.
Half-open admits only probes.
variants.hint: Are calls reaching the dependency freely?
variants.explanation: Closed is normal operation with measurement.

variants.title: Read the state
variants.context: Closed: calls reach the dependency while outcomes are recorded. Open: calls fail fast without reaching it. Half-open: a small number of probes pass and decide whether to close or reopen.
variants.prompt: The breaker returns a controlled error without contacting the dependency. Which state?
options: Half-open.
Open.
Closed.
optionFeedback: Half-open forwards some probes.
Open fails fast.
Closed forwards calls.
variants.hint: Is any call reaching the dependency?
variants.explanation: Open contains the failure; it does not repair the dependency.

variants.title: Read the state
variants.context: Closed: calls reach the dependency while outcomes are recorded. Open: calls fail fast without reaching it. Half-open: a small number of probes pass and decide whether to close or reopen.
variants.prompt: Three representative calls are allowed through and their outcomes will decide what happens next. Which state?
options: The half-open state.
The open state.
The closed state.
optionFeedback: Half-open probes recovery with bounded traffic.
Open admits nothing.
Closed admits everything.
variants.explanation: Half-open prevents a recovering service from being flooded.

variants.title: Open from evidence
variants.context: Open from evidence: a measurement window plus a minimum call count. Count connection failures, timeouts, and dependency 5xx; ignore business rejections; treat slow successes separately; record breaker rejections separately from dependency failures.
variants.prompt: A single failed call opens the breaker for the whole service. What is missing?
options: Nothing; one failed call is enough evidence to stop.
A minimum call count and a measurement window.
A longer open timer before the breaker probes again.
optionFeedback: One call is a sample of one, and a single fluke should not trip a breaker.
A tiny sample can produce a mathematically correct but operationally bad decision.
The timer sets how long it stays open, not whether opening was justified.
variants.hint: How many calls should inform the decision?
variants.explanation: Production breakers need both a window and a minimum count.

variants.title: Open from evidence
variants.context: Open from evidence: a measurement window plus a minimum call count. Count connection failures, timeouts, and dependency 5xx; ignore business rejections; treat slow successes separately; record breaker rejections separately from dependency failures.
variants.prompt: Invalid payment methods are counted as dependency failures and trip the breaker. What is wrong?
options: Business rejections must be ignored; the dependency answered fine.
Nothing; a failed call is a failed call whatever caused it.
Count them at half weight so they still influence the breaker.
optionFeedback: Only dependency failures belong in the window.
A rejected card is a correct answer from a healthy dependency.
Weighting still pollutes the signal.
variants.hint: Would retrying make this request succeed?
variants.explanation: Decide which outcomes count before deploying a breaker.

variants.title: Open from evidence
variants.context: Open from evidence: a measurement window plus a minimum call count. Count connection failures, timeouts, and dependency 5xx; ignore business rejections; treat slow successes separately; record breaker rejections separately from dependency failures.
variants.prompt: The dependency returns 200 but takes 8 seconds per call, exhausting caller threads. Does the failure-rate breaker help?
options: No breaker can help with a dependency that returns 200.
Not by itself; slow calls need their own boundary.
Yes; the failure-rate window already counts slow calls.
optionFeedback: A slow-call rate boundary addresses exactly this.
Treat slow successful calls separately from hard failures.
A slow 200 is still a success, so the failure-rate window never moves.
variants.hint: What does a successful-but-slow response do to the caller?
variants.explanation: Slow-call rate is a separate trip condition.

variants.title: Compose the controls
variants.context: Compose controls in order: bound one attempt with a timeout, retry only transient faults under a budget, stop repeated doomed calls with a breaker, reserve independent capacity with a bulkhead.
variants.prompt: A payment dependency degrades. Put the resilience controls in the order they act.

items.text: Retry: only transient faults, with backoff, jitter, idempotency, and one aggregate budget.
Timeout: stop waiting before the end-to-end budget is exhausted.
Bulkhead: keep one dependency from consuming every worker or connection.
Breaker: stop repeated doomed calls after enough recent evidence; retries stop when it rejects.

variants.hint: Each control protects a different boundary.
variants.explanation: Timeout → retry → breaker → bulkhead. Do not stack invisible retry policies across layers.

variants.title: Compose the controls
variants.context: Compose controls in order: bound one attempt with a timeout, retry only transient faults under a budget, stop repeated doomed calls with a breaker, reserve independent capacity with a bulkhead.
variants.prompt: A team adds resilience to a search dependency. Put the controls in order.

items.text: Open a breaker on evidence and make retries respect it.
Bound one attempt with a per-attempt timeout.
Retry classified transient failures under a retry budget.
Reserve independent capacity so search cannot starve checkout.

variants.hint: Retries must know about the breaker.
variants.explanation: Retry logic must stop when the breaker rejects, or the breaker is bypassed.

variants.title: Compose the controls
variants.context: Compose controls in order: bound one attempt with a timeout, retry only transient faults under a budget, stop repeated doomed calls with a breaker, reserve independent capacity with a bulkhead.
variants.prompt: SDK, mesh, and application each retry three times. Put the corrected design in order.

items.text: Isolate the dependency with a bulkhead.
Centralize retries in one layer under one budget.

variants.hint: Three retries at two layers can create nine dependency attempts.
variants.explanation: Invisible layered retries multiply load during an outage.

variants.title: Do the breaker math
variants.context: Open from evidence: a measurement window plus a minimum call count. Count connection failures, timeouts, and dependency 5xx; ignore business rejections; treat slow successes separately; record breaker rejections separately from dependency failures.
variants.prompt: Minimum calls is 20 and the failure-rate threshold is 50%. How many failures among the first 20 calls open the breaker?
variants.hint: Apply the threshold to the minimum sample.
variants.explanation: 10 of 20 is 50%, which reaches the threshold once the minimum count is met.

mistakes.feedback: Half of the sample is enough.
One failure is 5%, far below the threshold.

variants.title: Do the breaker math
variants.context: Compose controls in order: bound one attempt with a timeout, retry only transient faults under a budget, stop repeated doomed calls with a breaker, reserve independent capacity with a bulkhead.
variants.prompt: An SDK retries three times and a service mesh also retries three times, so each layer issues at most three attempts. How many dependency attempts can one call create?
variants.explanation: 3 × 3 = 9 attempts, which is why retries belong in one layer with one budget.

mistakes.feedback: Retries multiply across layers rather than add.
Each mesh attempt can trigger three SDK attempts.

variants.title: Do the breaker math
variants.context: Time passing is permission to test, not proof of recovery. Probes must be representative and bounded; a shallow health endpoint gives false confidence; reopen immediately when the recovery contract fails.
variants.prompt: Half-open admits 3 probes and requires all to succeed. Two succeed and one is slow. How many probes reached the dependency?
variants.hint: All admitted probes reach the dependency; any failure reopens.
variants.explanation: Three probes ran. The slow one fails the recovery contract, so the breaker reopens and waits before the next probe cohort.

mistakes.feedback: The slow probe still reached the dependency.
Half-open admits probes; that is its purpose.

variants.title: Recover with evidence
variants.context: Time passing is permission to test, not proof of recovery. Probes must be representative and bounded; a shallow health endpoint gives false confidence; reopen immediately when the recovery contract fails.
variants.prompt: The open timer expired. Has the dependency recovered?
options: Yes, if the timer was long enough for a restart.
Unknown; the timer only grants permission to probe.
Yes; the timer is set to the dependency's recovery time.
optionFeedback: A longer wait is still waiting, and waiting produces no evidence.
Recovery needs new evidence from representative probes.
The timer encodes a guess about recovery, and a guess is not a measurement.
variants.explanation: Half-open exists to test recovery without flooding.

variants.title: Recover with evidence
variants.context: Time passing is permission to test, not proof of recovery. Probes must be representative and bounded; a shallow health endpoint gives false confidence; reopen immediately when the recovery contract fails.
variants.prompt: Probes hit a shallow /health endpoint that returns 200 while real reads still time out. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; a 200 from /health means the service is healthy.
The probe should treat 204 rather than 200 as recovery.
Probes must exercise the same path and capacity as real traffic.
optionFeedback: Health endpoints often bypass the failing path.
Which status code counts as success does not change what the probe measured.
A shallow endpoint produces false confidence.
variants.hint: Does the probe touch what real traffic touches?

variants.title: Recover with evidence
variants.context: Time passing is permission to test, not proof of recovery. Probes must be representative and bounded; a shallow health endpoint gives false confidence; reopen immediately when the recovery contract fails.
variants.prompt: An open breaker’s rejections are being counted as dependency failures, keeping it open. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; a rejected call is a failure the caller experienced.
Lower the failure threshold so the breaker closes sooner.
Breaker rejections are caller policy, not fresh dependency evidence.
optionFeedback: A rejected call never reached the dependency.
A different threshold cannot help while the window feeds on its own rejections.
Counting rejections creates a self-sustaining open state.
variants.hint: Did the rejected call reach the dependency?
variants.explanation: Record breaker rejections separately from dependency failures.
